text: `curl http://db:8080/` fails to resolve. Check whether the *record* is actually the problem: `dig +short @127.0.0.1 db.internal.example`. It resolves fine to `127.0.0.1` -- so the DNS data itself is correct. The problem must be in how the short name `db` gets turned into a full name to look up.
When you look up a bare name like `db` (no dot in it), the resolver doesn't ask for `db` as-is -- it appends a *search domain* from `/etc/resolv.conf` first. Look at it: `cat /etc/resolv.conf`.

The `search` line points at `prod.example.com`, which turns `db` into `db.prod.example.com` -- a zone that doesn't exist here. The real internal zone (confirmed by your `dig` in hint 1) is `internal.example`. This is exactly the kind of thing that gets left behind after an internal zone rename: the DNS records got migrated, but this host's resolver config didn't.

Fix the search domain. `/etc/resolv.conf` is a bind-mounted file, so `sed -i` fails with 'Device or resource busy' (it can't do its rename trick) -- edit it in place with `sudo nano /etc/resolv.conf` and change `search prod.example.com` to `search internal.example`, or rewrite it without a rename: `sudo sh -c "printf 'nameserver 127.0.0.1\nsearch internal.example\n' > /etc/resolv.conf"`. Re-test `curl http://db:8080/`.
